newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian bank results to be eyed for merger clues.
newsitem.headline: Belgian bank results to be eyed for merger clues.

text.p: Belgium's top four listed banks are set to publish their best earnings for years this month, but analysts said they would be more interested in any comments about possible mergers or partnerships in the industry.

Even though last year's low short-term yields, falling bond yields and historically steep yield curve should allow banks to publish earnings growth of 20 percent or more, analysts expected banks will manage their profit and loss accounts so as to show earnings growth between 10 and 15 percent.

Forecasts for profit growth ranged from nine to 16 percent. Analysts said that much will depend on how much the banks set aside for the cost of switching to the euro and for the adaptation of computer systems to cope with the millenium date change.

"The bigger question is what the role of Belgian banks in a euro-environment will be. Some merger and acquisiton activity is possible, notably involving Generale Bank or BBL," said Credit Suisse First Boston bank analyst Mark Hoge.

Banque Bruxelles Lambert (BBL) will kick off the listed banks' earnings season on Wednesday. The occasion will be financial markets' first chance to hear what new chief executive officer Michel Tilmant, who took over in January, thinks about his bank's future.
Tilmant has so far declined to comment on a well-publicised statement by his predecessor Daniel Cardon that BBL will need a partner to face the challenge of the single currency.

In January, Etienne Davignon, Chairman of Generale Bank parent company Ste Generale de Belgique SA (SGB), said the idea of a merger between Generale Bank and BBL was still an attractive business proposition.
Talks about possible cooperation early in 1996 broke off because of opposition from BBL shareholder Internationale Nederlanden Groep (ING).
Generale Bank publishes 1996 earnings on March 11. Its chief executive officer Ferdinand Chaffart has repeatedly said that he sees no need for a partner. But some fellow bankers disagree.

Philippe Romagnoli, chief executive officer of unlisted Paribas Bank Belgium, said last week that it would be desirable for at least two, if not three, major Belgian banks to merge to create an institution with total assets of at least 15,000 billion Belgian francs or $500 billion.

At the end of 1995, Generale Bank, Belgium's biggest, had assets of 4,739 billion francs ($135 billion), less than half those of Dutch market leader ABN Amro's, whose 1996 assets totalled $311 billion.

Given these numbers, Belgian banks can only dream of high-profile international takeovers, such as ABN Amro's 1992 purchase of British stockbroker Hoare Govett or ING's acquisition of collapsed British merchant bank Barings in 1995, analysts said.

Local authority lender Credit Communal/Gemeentekrediet (CCB), Belgium's second-biggest bank, is so far the only major Belgian player which has teamed up with a foreign player -- French Credit Local de France. The two banks, which work together internationally under the Dexia brand, last month announced a major Italian acquisition.
"CCB is one of the few Belgian banks with a foreign growth strategy," BBL analyst Tony Depoortere said. "Our top banks are too small. They need economies of scale," he added.
CCB's results are due on April 2.
Belgium's Kredietbank, whose marketing slogan is "The bank from here", has so far concentrated on picking up smaller domestic rivals and minority stakes in banks in emerging markets.
But its independent stance has not prevented its shares from seeing the occasional bout of speculative buying, notably on one rumour it was investigating a link with Credit Commercial de France.
Kredietbank, which is controlled by holding company Almanij, is due to release results on March 13.

Lower down the league, smaller, non-listed, banks are also working on their size. BACOB, a cooperative bank owned by Belgium's christian democratic workers' movement, said last week it was looking for a foreign partner in France, Germany, the Netherlands or Austria.
Belgian cooperative bank CERA announced recently it would take over Bank Indosuez Belgium.
-- Geert De Clercq, Brussels Newsroom +32 2 287 6813, Fax +32 2 230 7710
